children: Hungary's inflation inched up to 1.3% in August, data showed on Tuesday, and while that was well below the central bank's 3% target, some analysts say falls in the forint and global bond market volatility may make policymakers cautious on rate cuts.

Headline inflation (HUCPIY=ECI) rose to 1.3% from 1.2% in July, coming in a touch below analysts' forecasts for a 1.4% annual increase. Core inflation (HUCPIC=ECI) ran at 2%, in line with market forecasts and also below the bank's target.

Last month the central bank delivered its third successive quarter-point rate cut, as expected, to 5.5%, and left the door open to further rate easing depending on its September inflation projections and global market developments.

ING economist Peter Virovacz said the inflation data alone would allow the central bank to proceed with rate easing, but the benign print has been partly overshadowed by unfavourable market developments since the bank's August policy meeting.
"The key factor will be how the central bank sees the forint's weakening, the increase in energy prices and the rise in global bond yields," he said.

"Knowing their cautious approach, I can easily see a brief pause in rate easing, but I think two more rate cuts should still be possible around the end of the year," he said, projecting the base rate at 5% at the end of 2026.

, which scaled five-year highs after centre-right Prime Minister Peter Magyar's April election victory, fell to its lowest levels this month since Magyar took power as the Middle East conflict put markets under pressure.

Investors drove Polish and Czech 10-year bond yields to more than three-year highs amid a global market selloff, with growth in Hungarian yields contained by pledges by Magyar to curb the budget deficit and put Hungary on course to adopting the euro.
The bank's next rate meeting is due on September 22, when it will also publish a new batch of quarterly economic forecasts.
